title: Anchoring and First Offers
description: The first specific number placed on the table pulls the entire negotiation toward itself, even when the number is arbitrary.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: The first specific number placed on the table pulls the entire negotiation toward itself, even when the number is arbitrary.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A seller lists a house at $520,000. Buyers then evaluate $490,000 as a 'deal,' even if the market value is $470,000.
A candidate says, 'I'm targeting $95,000.' The hiring manager's counter lands near $88,000—much higher than the original budget of $80,000.

sections.title: Typical Behaviors
content: The party who anchors speaks first and with specificity: 'Based on my research, $76,400.'
The receiving party blinks, hesitates, or reflexively counter-offers near the anchor instead of resetting the frame.

sections.title: Warning Signs You Are Being Anchored
content: The other side throws out a number and waits silently.
The anchor is framed as 'industry standard' or 'what we always pay.'

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Do not counter off their anchor. Instead, reframe: 'That doesn't match the data I've seen. Let's look at comparable deals.'
Mentally set your own target and boundaries before hearing any numbers.

sections.title: Common Mistake
sections.content: Countering by immediately saying 'That's too high/low.' Any reaction that acknowledges the anchor solidifies its power.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: The first number is a magnet. If you don't want to be pulled, don't place your counter on its axis.
